new_groups.label: Letters on the squadron before Tripoli, sent to Congress
new_groups.definition: Two letters on the American squadron's attacks on Tripoli in August and September 1804, as the 1805 papers printed them after the President sent them to Congress: Richard O'Brien's letter from Malta of 5 September 1804 (sent on 31 December 1804) and Commodore Preble's letter of 18 September 1804 (sent on 20 February 1805). Contains those two groups. Each is an American official's own account.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1805 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: O'Brien's letter from Malta on the attacks on Tripoli
new_groups.definition: Printings of the letter of Richard O'Brien, 'late Consul of the United States, at Algiers', to John Gavino, consul at Gibraltar, dated Malta, 5 September 1804, 'giving some details of transactions before Tripoli', which the President communicated to Congress on 31 December 1804: the American gun boats and two bombards 'entered the harbour of Tripoli, and within 600 feet of the Bashaw's castle' began their attack. An American official's own account.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1805 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: Commodore Preble's letter of 18 September 1804
new_groups.definition: Printings of the letter of Commodore Edward Preble to the Secretary of the Navy, from the harbour of Malta, 18 September 1804, which the President sent to Congress with his message of 20 February 1805: 'I had the honor to write you from Messina, under date of the 5th of July', followed by his day-by-day account of the squadron before Tripoli. The commander's own account.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1805 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: The impeachment trial of Judge Chase, 1805
new_groups.definition: Four printed pieces of the trial of Samuel Chase, an associate justice of the Supreme Court, before the Senate on the articles of impeachment exhibited by the House of Representatives, as the 1805 papers printed them: his speech of 2 January, his answer and pleas of 4 February, the House's replication, and the declaration of 1 March that he was acquitted. Contains those four groups. Each side's words are its own: the speech and the answer are the accused judge's, the replication the House's.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1805 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: Judge Chase's speech to the Senate, 2 January
new_groups.definition: Printings of the speech of Samuel Chase before the Senate sitting as a court of impeachment, 2 January 1805: 'I appear, in obedience to a summons from this honorable court, to answer articles of impeachment exhibited against me'; he asks for time until the next session to prepare his answer. The accused judge's own words.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1805 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: The answer and pleas of Samuel Chase, 4 February
new_groups.definition: Printings of 'The answer, and pleas of Samuel Chase, one of the associate justices of the supreme court of the United States, to the articles of impeachment exhibited against him', given in the Senate on 4 February 1805: 'This respondent, in his proper person, comes into the said court, and protesting that there is no high crime or misdemeanor particularly alleged'. A long document printed in parts; the accused judge's own defence.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1805 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: The House's replication to Judge Chase's answer
new_groups.definition: Printings of the replication of the House of Representatives to the answer of Samuel Chase, reported by its managers and adopted by the House in February 1805: 'The House of Representatives of the United States have considered the answer of Samuel Chase, one of the associate justices of the supreme court of the United States, to the articles of impeachment'. The accusers' own reply.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1805 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: The declaration that Judge Chase is acquitted, 1 March
new_groups.definition: Printings of the declaration made on 1 March 1805 by the President of the Senate, after the votes on the eight articles, as the papers' accounts of the court quote it: 'there not being a constitutional majority on any one article, it becomes my duty to pronounce that Samuel Chase, Esq. is acquitted', or, in the National Intelligencer's account, 'Hence it appears that there is not a constitutional majority of votes finding Samuel Chase, Esquire, guilty, on any one article'. The declaration as each account quotes it.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1805 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: President Jefferson's second inaugural address
new_groups.definition: Printings of the speech President Thomas Jefferson delivered on taking the oath of office for a second term, 4 March 1805: 'Proceeding, fellow citizens, to that qualification which the constitution requires, before my entrance on the charge again conferred on me'. He gives his account of his first term: taxes and the debt, Louisiana, 'the aboriginal inhabitants of these countries', religion and the press. The President's own account (a policy argument).
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1805 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: Napoleon's letter to the King of England

new_groups.label: Lord Mulgrave's answer to Talleyrand

new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1805 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: News of the peace with Tripoli, 1805
new_groups.definition: How the peace with Tripoli of June 1805 reached the papers from late August: the Salem Register's report of news from Naples, and the letters released at Washington in September: Commodore Rodgers's letter on the peace, with the government's notice, Captain Hull's letter on the attack on Derne and Commodore Barron's letter to William Eaton. Contains those four groups.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1805 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: Salem report: news from Naples by the brig Belle-Isle
new_groups.definition: Printings of a report from the Salem Register of 29 August 1805: 'Yesterday the brig Belle-Isle, Capt. Leach, arrived here in 66 days from Naples. About eight days before he sailed, news arrived there, that Gen. Eaton, at the head of the small American force which had been detached from our Mediterranean squadron, and the troops collected by the rival brother of the Bashaw of Tripoli, had had an engagement'. News heard at Naples, reported at second hand.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1805 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: The official notice of peace with Tripoli and Commodore Rodgers's letter
new_groups.definition: Printings of the government's notice of September 1805, 'Preliminaries of peace with Tripoli were signed on the second day of June last, and on the same day capt. The commodore's name is printed 'Rodgers' or 'Rogers'. The government's notice and the commander's own account.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1805 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: Captain Hull's letter on the attack on Derne
new_groups.definition: Printings of 'a copy of a letter from capt. An officer's own account of the attack on Derne.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1805 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: Commodore Barron's letter to William Eaton, 22 March
new_groups.definition: Printings of 'an extract of a letter from Commodore Barron to William Eaton, Esq. dated Malta, March 22, 1805', released at Washington in September: 'You must be sensible that in giving their sanction to a co-operation with the Ex-Bashaw, government did not contemplate the measure as leading necessarily and absolutely to a re-instatement of that Prince'; he withholds his sanction from any convention binding the United States to place the Ex-Bashaw on the throne. new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1805 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: Admiral Calder's dispatch on the action of 22 July
new_groups.definition: Printings of the dispatch of Vice-Admiral Sir Robert Calder to Admiral Cornwallis, 'Prince of Wales, July 23, 1805', from the London Gazette: 'Yesterday at noon ... I was favored with a view of the combined squadrons of France and Spain, consisting of 20 sail of the line'; he 'brought on an action which lasted upwards of four hours' and took two ships. The British commander's own account.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1805 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: British orders on American vessels carrying colonial produce, 1805
new_groups.definition: Two items on British orders concerning American vessels that carried the produce of the enemy's colonies, as the papers printed them from September 1805: a London paragraph of 7 and 8 August reporting an order to detain such vessels, and the Privy Council's minute of 3 August as the British consuls published it in November. Contains those two groups.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1805 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: London paragraph: an order to detain American vessels
new_groups.definition: Printings of a London newspaper paragraph of 7 or 8 August 1805: 'An order, we understand, was sent to all the out ports some days ago, instructing our cruisers to detain all American vessels which have on board property not the produce of the United States. This order has been already acted upon'. A report ('we understand', 'it is said'); the reason it gives is the London paper's. The paragraph of 7 August ('we understand', 'not the produce') and of 8 August ('it is said', 'not the property') are counted together.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1805 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: The Privy Council's minute of 3 August, published by the British consuls
new_groups.definition: Printings of the minute of the Lords of the British Privy Council of 3 August 1805 on the trade carried on in neutral ships, as the British consuls published it to American merchants in November: their Lordships resolved 'to allow the trade with the settlements and islands, belonging to the enemy, in America and the West Indies, to be carried on through the medium of the British free ports in the West Indies, and not otherwise', with an exception for ships cleared from the Havana before 1 November. Three consuls' notices are counted together: the consul general's at Philadelphia, the consul's for Virginia and the consul general's at New York, the last two with an 'Extract of Council Minute'. Britain's own document.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1805 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: Reports from Algiers, 1805
new_groups.definition: Two items from Algiers printed from September to November 1805: a Salem report, by way of Leghorn, of an insurrection at Algiers, and the letter of 9 September of the American charge d'affaires at Algiers that 'the soldiers rose in a body and murdered the Dey'. Contains those two groups.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1805 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: Salem report: Captain Shillaber's news of an insurrection at Algiers
new_groups.definition: Printings of a Salem report of September 1805, headed in most papers 'Bloody Scenes at Algiers': 'Capt. Shillaber, from Leghorn, informs us, that on the 7th July a brig arrived there from Algiers, and brought accounts of an insurrection at that place'; a Leghorn letter of 8 July follows. News at third hand: a shipmaster repeats what a brig brought to Leghorn.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1805 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: Mountford's letter from Algiers, 9 September
new_groups.definition: Printings of a letter dated 'Algiers, September 9, 1805', from Mr. Mountford, 'secretary of Mr. Lear, and now our charge d'affaires at Algiers', which General Eaton gave to the Enquirer: 'I have only a few moments to inform you, our affairs here are well. On the 30th ult. the soldiers rose in a body and murdered the Dey and his prime minister.' An American official's own short report; the words are his.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1805 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: A Paris article of 31 August on the Austrian armies
new_groups.definition: Printings of a Paris article dated 31 August 1805, from French and Dutch papers: 'The frontiers of the empire seem to be menaced by the movements of the Austrian armies. Thirty thousand men are to march from the camps of Boulogne to the banks of the Rhine'; it blames the British cabinet for the war and warns that 'there is in future more than one day of Marengo to France and Austria'. One government's side, in a Paris paper: argument and warning.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1805 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: Washington paragraph on a treaty with the chiefs of the Creek Nation
new_groups.definition: Printings of a paragraph of the National Intelligencer of 18 November 1805: 'A very advantageous TREATY has been made, we understand, at this place, with the chiefs of the Creek Nation; by which a large cession of land is made to the United States, and the right given to open a direct road to New Orleans'. The government paper's report ('we understand'); 'very advantageous' is its own judgement.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1805 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: Napoleon's speech to the French Senate, September 1805
new_groups.definition: Printings of the speech of the Emperor Napoleon to the French Senate in September 1805, from Paris papers: 'Senators, In the present circumstances of Europe, I feel the necessity of appearing in the midst of you, and of making known to you my sentiments'; he is about to leave his capital to put himself at the head of the army. A head of state's own account. The Norfolk Gazette prints another translation ('I come among you to communicate my sentiments'), counted with the others.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1805 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: A royal order from Madrid on American vessels carried into Algeziras
new_groups.definition: Printings of a royal order dated 'Madrid, Sept. 3, 1805' (5 September in some papers), as the Spanish commander of marine at Algeziras received it and a Gibraltar paper printed it: 'His Excellency, the Minister of the United States, has complained of new grievances and captures of American vessels by the Spanish privateers; and that eleven Americans have been carried into Algeziras'; vessels taken only for carrying English goods are to be released. The Spanish government's own order, at second hand.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1805 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: The President's message to Congress, 3 December 1805
new_groups.definition: Printings of President Jefferson's annual message to Congress of 3 December 1805: 'At a moment when the nations of Europe are in commotion and arming against each other, and when those with whom we have principal intercourse are engaging the resources of commerce in their contest'. He speaks of injuries to American commerce, of Spain and the territories of Orleans and the Mississippi, of gun boats and the militia, the peace with Tripoli, the Indian nations and the Treasury. The executive's own account and recommendations.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1805 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: Admiral Collingwood's dispatch on the action off Cape Trafalgar
new_groups.definition: Printings of the London Gazette Extraordinary of 6 November 1805: 'Dispatches, of which the following are copies, were received at the Admiralty this day at one o'clock A. M. from vice-admiral Collingwood', with his dispatch 'Euryalus, off Cape Trafalgar, Oct. 22': 'The ever to be lamented death of vice-admiral lord viscount Nelson, who, in the late conflict with the enemy, fell in the hour of victory'. The British commander's own account.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1805 printings, checked against the scan.

dispositions_summary.method: The automatic families first printed in 1805 that reach 4 or more papers, long-running ones included (story_items.py --long-running), were split into single printed items (items.json: 99 items in 7 or more papers by the finder's count, 15 in 9). Because some documents first printed in late 1804 reach the 1805 pages (the Chase impeachment, the acts of the session, Preble's letter), the script was also run with year 1804 over the 1805 pages (items_from_1804.json). The 1805 pages are those the base release dates to 1805 (year_search_pages.py --printed-dates), which adds the Kentucky Gazette issue of 28 May 1805 that the collection files under 1807. Two AI readers each read the items of half the year and proposed stories; their proposals were merged and checked here, and each item's printings were looked for with phrase searches over all 3,811 pages in both transcriptions (phrase_patterns.json, phrase_hits.json; keys that start 'candidate:' are items not admitted). Papers with pages in a story's weeks but no printing were searched with loose keywords; the scan pages whose RevX text is filed under another page were read in the CA transcription. Every admitted printing was then checked against its page scan (SCAN_PROTOCOL.md, scan_points.json).
dispositions_summary.selection_rule: As for 1776, 1807 and 1808: every single item printed in 9 or more newspapers was admitted, except digests of unrelated paragraphs; items in 7 or 8 papers were chosen to cover the months and the main kinds of news. Every story alike (the owner's rule of 11 November 2026): no item was left out for its subject. Stories are counted item by item; where one publication holds several documents, or several documents belong to one affair, each is its own group under a parent story. A sub-story may have fewer than 7 papers when its parent reaches 7. The Portland Gazette's three titles of 1805 (Jenks' Portland Gazette, Portland Gazette, Portland Gazette and Maine Advertiser) count as one newspaper; no story's count depends on two of them.
